name: Parenthetical Clause Usage
description: Analyzes the frequency and complexity of parenthetical injections—such as text within parentheses (like this), em-dashes—like this—or set off by commas. AI models tend to use parentheticals strictly for dry, explanatory clarification, whereas humans frequently use them to inject spontaneous personal opinion, sarcasm, or secondary, tangential thoughts that break the main sentence's logical flow.
algorithm: Syntactic Branching and Parenthetical Semantic Drift Analysis
mechanism: This algorithm uses dependency parsing and regex to isolate all parenthetical structures (parentheses, brackets, and em-dash clauses) within the text. It evaluates two core metrics: frequency and semantic distance. Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained to be highly cohesive and straightforward; they rarely interrupt their own train of thought. When an AI does use a parenthetical, it is almost exclusively for defining terms (e.g., 'the Federal Reserve (Fed)') or citing dates (e.g., 'George Washington (1732–1799)'). Human writers, by contrast, frequently experience 'mid-sentence realizations'—interrupting their core thought to inject a tangential joke, a qualifying doubt, or a completely separate sub-plot before returning to the main verb. The system measures the 'Semantic Drift' of the parenthetical clause compared to the main sentence. A high frequency of simple, definitional parentheticals indicates machine alignment, while complex, tangential interruptions strongly suggest organic human cognitive processing.
useCase: Highly effective for analyzing conversational writing, blog posts, and opinion pieces, distinguishing the sterile, explanatory parentheticals of an AI from the spontaneous, interruptive, and often messy parentheticals of a human writer.
strengths:
• Excellent at detecting human 'stream of consciousness' writing styles, which LLMs struggle to organically replicate without explicit prompting.
• Highly accurate in identifying the classic AI hallmark of over-defining simple acronyms or concepts in parentheses.
limitations:
• Susceptible to false positives when analyzing highly technical, academic, or legal documents, where humans are forced to use parentheticals solely for citations, acronym definitions, or rigid clarifications.
• Less effective on very short texts where parentheticals simply do not occur.
parameters:
Analysis: Regex Bracket/Dash Extraction and Dependency Parsing
Metric: Parenthetical Frequency and Semantic Drift Variance
Output: 0-100 Syntactic Interruption (Artificiality) Score
accuracy: Moderate to High — 70-80% accuracy. A strong, nuanced signal for differentiating spontaneous human thought from highly planned, linear AI generation.

references.title: Manning, C.D. & Schütze, H. (1999). Foundations of Statistical Natural Language Processing. MIT Press.
Uchendu, A. et al. (2020). Authorship Attribution for Neural Text Generation. EMNLP.
